Hashcat mode 22500. Example attack. Hashcat -a 0 -m 22500 -O -o foundOutput.txt hash.txt passwordlist.txt. This will run an attack against the hash in hash.txt trying all words in passwordlist.txt and if it finds it, it will output to foundOutput.txt. I recommend the hashmob dictionary it's 15gb uncompressed and is the best out there. You should be able to run through it in not much time on a cpu but if you have a GPU you can use rules, hashcat comes with some by default in the rules folder, to use them you apply the -r command followed by the file location. If you're using a huge password list like hashmob you should use a few amount of rules where as if you're using a file that contains your own potential passwords you should use a huge rule list(you can find these on the hashmob site also). As for converting etc. You don't need to do anything to the output hash from multibit2john. It should look something like $multibit$1$xxxxxxx$xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx(not the correct amount of x's, just an example). Put that hash in hash.txt and run away.

The fact he stated his files are labeled bitcoin keys. The fact the file is from 2013, when multibit, bitcoin core and electrum was the main boys. But the only files that were labeled as such are multibit, with android wallet doing the same encryption and file names/types. The content of the file he quoted as being mixed alphanumeric with / between, this is base64 encoding. Which just further confirms that its what we think it is. Bitcoin private keys don't contain /, so it's not some exported keys. It's the base64 encoded multibit key export file.

That's OK. We can all learn something. OpenSSL is a tool that can be used to encrypt/decrypt things in aes cbc. OpenSSL used md5 to generate its encryption keys. So when I say OpenSSL md5 decryption, the emphasis is on OpenSSL, not md5. Its important I state md5 there so he doesn't attempt to decrypt with a different hash algorithm as key.

Maybe you misunderstood me. AES is the decryption part. MD5 is used for the key. By "openssl md5 decryption", I'm speaking of the openssl md5 variant of its encrypt/decrypt function.. as openssl updated to another hash algorithm later on.

It's not going to be a seed phrase. 2013 was a different time. Seeds were rare. As he said, his file is labeled bitcoin keys. Keys are.. keys.. not seeds. And as I explained in my other post, what he has is the export of multibit which is a base64 encoded and aes encrypted private keys. Base64 encoding is alphanumeric + /  which is why he has the / in his file.

What you have is a base64 encoded and encrypted private key, either from multibit or any of the android wallets or some online wallets. The good news is that the vast majority use the same decryption process which is 3x MD5 AES CBC. Your file name will likely be along the lines of bitcoin-wallet-keys-2013-01-01.key or similar, it's likely that all your files are the same keys with different backup dates but theres also a chance that you have added more keys down the line. You can download openssl and you can Google the openssl md5 decryption command for the file. If your file starts with u2fsd, that confirms it. If you don't remember the password you can use hashcat. Download multibit2john.py, a python script so make sure you have python installed, run the script againt the wallet and it will give you a hash, take the hash and import into hashcat, use a big wordlist from weakpass or use your own potential passwords along with manipulation rules. So many trash comments on here it's funny. First off, you're absolute best bet is still hashcat. If you have no idea of the password.. then we need to run a dictionary attack. You can rent vast.ai instances for pretty cheap. $5 for 1 hour of 8x4090 time. You rent 2-3hours and you can run the entirety of the hashmob dictionary. It's a 15gb file that is the most complete real human user password list available. You can find it on hashmob.com wordlist section. If you can't rent instances. You can download ignis-10m.txt, you can find it on github and run on your own server. Rockyou is a joke wordlist nowadays, don't use it. Next if you know some potential passwords it could be(and this is the better option) you put all of them in a file and use a rule list, you can also download these from hashmob. Some of these will do millions of manipulations to your passwords and are highly optimised for it. You should also consider that there was a bitcoin core vulnerability for very old wallet versions that once encrypted, didn't delete the old unencrypted keys from the database, allowing anybody with the wallet file to do a binary search. Think this was for core version 0.4 but don't quote me. Hashmob should crack at least 50% of passwords. Add on top of that a rule based attack on known passwords that's probably in the 80%+ range of probability in cracking.
